tldr: This paper demonstrates that popular memory-augmented robot policies (VLAs), which uniformly downsample frames across an episode and timestamp them, fall into a shortcut learning trap: they mistake the mere passage of time for actual task progress, even when no real work was done.
hero_caption: Simply inserting a pause or wrist fidget that does not affect task progress makes the policy mistake waiting for work and stop early (Visible). However, withholding those same frames from memory restores the success rate completely under the same physical interruption (Hidden), revealing that the real issue is time-based memory, not physical disturbance.
overview:
Memory-augmented Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, which recall past actions and observations, are actively studied today. For instance, in a task like "move a cube three times, then press a button," the current view alone cannot tell you which repetition you are on, so past memory is essential. A common way to implement this memory is to sample frames uniformly across the episode and attach time embeddings (timestamps). It seems like a neat design that keeps computational cost fixed.

However, in the real world, robots routinely encounter meaningless intervals (null events) where no task progress occurs—such as pausing for safety stops, waiting for planner computations, or hesitating with minor wrist twitches. If a robot's memory is simply filled by elapsed time, can it tell waiting from working?

When the authors tested representative policies on the RoboMME benchmark, the answer was "not at all." Pausing for just a few seconds or fidgeting the wrist made the policy hallucinate that work was done, pressing the button to stop before reaching the target count (the authors term this "phantom progress"). Through careful causal interventions, they traced this failure to a temporal shortcut: because training demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress. Furthermore, even removing timestamps does not fix the issue, because null event frames still occupy time-sampled memory slots. Thus, a true fix requires indexing memory by state changes in the world (events) rather than by clock ticks.
contributions: First identifying and formulating "phantom progress," where task-irrelevant waiting or idle motions (null events) cause time-based memory VLA policies to mistake time for completed work and stop early.

Proving through causal interventions (rescaling timestamps, withholding frames) that policies rely on elapsed time itself as a proxy for progress (a temporal shortcut), rather than on actual event occurrences.
Showing that completely removing explicit timestamps fails to solve the problem, because occupying time-sampled memory slots still implicitly represents elapsed time and triggers the same failure.

Demonstrating that while data augmentation (injecting pauses) impairs counting and fails as a fundamental fix, applying an event-driven index based on world state changes and loop closures at inference time recovers substantial robustness without retraining.

sections.heading: Working or just waiting? Doubting the robot's memory
sections.summary: Past memory is essential for tasks requiring repeated counting, and uniform time-sampled memory is widely used. However, inserting "do-nothing intervals" (null events) that make zero task progress slashes the success rate of state-of-the-art policies, causing them to terminate before finishing the required counts.
sections.details:
Many manipulation tasks cannot be solved from the current observation alone. For example, in a task where a robot must lift a cube three times and then press a button, what the robot sees right before lifting the second time is almost identical to what it sees before the third time. The robot must therefore remember how many times it has already lifted the cube. To tackle this, memory-augmented VLAs have been proposed to store past episode history. A standard and strong design among them samples frames uniformly across the episode and stamps each frame with an absolute time step.

However, in real-world deployment, robots frequently encounter meaningless intervals with zero task progress (null events)—such as waiting for safety clearances, planner delays, or swinging in the air. A memory meant to remember what happened should simply ignore and skip these blank intervals.

Yet when the authors tested FrameSamp-Modul, the top-performing released policy on the RoboMME benchmark, the results were striking. Simply pausing the robot twice for 5 seconds (pause) or rotating its wrist back and forth (wrist fidget) caused the success count out of 50 episodes to plummet from 47 to 16 on PickXtimes, and from 44 to 10 on SwingXtimes. Nearly 100% of these failures were "early stops," where the robot pressed the button before completing the required counts. In short, the robot mistook empty waiting intervals for work done. The authors call this phenomenon "phantom progress."

sections.heading: Robot memory, shortcut learning, and redundancy reduction
sections.summary: This work sits at the intersection of memory mechanisms for robot policies, shortcut learning in imitation learning, and video summarization. While existing robustness benchmarks focused strictly on visual and geometric perturbations, this paper investigates the overlooked blind spot of temporal disruptions at inference time.
sections.details:
### Memory in Robot Policies
Many VLAs take only the current frame or a short frame stack as input. For long-horizon tasks, researchers have proposed transformer history models, perceptual memory banks, keyframe selection, and recurrent or test-time adaptive memory. Benchmarks like RoboMME have competed over which memory architecture scores highest, but very few studies causally examine what the memory is actually looking at. While prior work treated this as a history distribution shift, this paper sets itself apart by identifying elapsed time as the concrete confounding factor and proving through interventions that the policy reads it.

### Shortcut Learning and Time in Imitation Learning
Shortcuts in imitation learning (causal confusion or simply copying past actions) have long been known. Elapsed time in particular can be a legitimate state variable in time-constrained tasks, making policies prone to overfitting on it. In video recognition, researchers have also pointed out biases where models answer questions based on the temporal position of a moment rather than video content. This work exposes how temporal position acts as a substitute for content in memory-augmented robot VLAs.

### Video Memory Redundancy and Robustness
To compress long videos, methods prune frames based on visual similarity (frame merging or event segmentation). However, they judge redundancy by pixel changes. A null event like a wrist fidget changes the image drastically in every frame, so appearance-based pruning cannot remove it. Furthermore, conventional robot robustness evaluations only perturb camera poses, lighting, textures, or language instructions. No prior work has tested temporal disruptions that insert null events at test time.

sections.heading: Behind the scenes: Benchmarks, null events, and the testing protocol
sections.summary: Using counting tasks (PickXtimes, SwingXtimes) in the RoboMME simulation environment, the authors evaluated the top-performing FrameSamp models. They defined three null events that do not affect task progress, and compared a Visible condition (where frames are written to memory) with a Hidden condition (where the physical action happens, but frames are withheld from memory).
sections.details:
### Tasks and Evaluated Policies
The evaluation uses two counting tasks from RoboMME. One is "PickXtimes," where the robot picks and places a cube $K$ times (1 to 5 times) and then presses a button. The other is "SwingXtimes," where the robot swings a cube back and forth between two target locations $K$ times (1 to 3 times). As baselines, the authors evaluate released models (MME-VLA) built on OpenPI's $\pi_{0.5}$. The standard "FrameSamp" retains 32 frames uniformly sampled across the episode, stamping each frame with a sinusoidal absolute step encoding. There are three variants: Modul (read via cross-attention), Expert (using a separate expert), and In-context. FrameSamp-Modul, which achieves the highest score, is the primary target.

### Three Null Events (Meaningless Intervals)
At action chunk boundaries of the policy (steps 48 and 160), three types of events are inserted that do not affect the task object:
- **Pause**: The robot remains completely stationary for 100 environment steps (5 seconds).
- **Wrist fidget**: The robot's wrist rotates back and forth within $\pm 0.3$ rad for 100 steps while holding position (arm and environment stay unchanged).
- **Air-grasp**: The gripper opens and closes above the object and returns to its initial pose.

### Causal Isolation: Visible vs. Hidden Conditions
To distinguish whether failure stems from physical factors (arm drift from pausing) or memory factors (recording dead time), the authors compare two conditions:
- **Visible**: As usual, frames during null events are sampled into memory, and timestamps advance.
- **Hidden**: The robot executes the exact same 5-second pause or wrist fidget in the simulator, but those frames are withheld from memory, and timestamps pause.
All tests run across 50 episodes with identical seeds, rigorously evaluated using paired binomial tests (McNemar's test).

sections.heading: Phantom progress: Empty intervals make the robot think it worked
sections.summary: Pausing for 5 seconds or fidgeting the wrist devastates success rates, and almost all failures are early button presses before reaching the required count. However, withholding the interruption frames from memory (Hidden) completely restores the success rate under the exact same physical motion, proving the issue lies in memory itself.
sections.details:
Injecting null events into the released policy revealed striking vulnerability. Pausing twice for 5 seconds slashed success from 47 to 16 on PickXtimes and from 44 to 10 on SwingXtimes (Figure F2). Wrist fidgeting caused identical drops to 16 and 10, and air-grasping halved success on SwingXtimes. Moreover, pausing for just 1.5 seconds triggered most of this performance drop.

Crucially, consider how the robot failed. If physical interruption merely confused the controller, random failures such as dropping cubes or over-repeating should have increased. Instead, nearly 100% of recorded failures were early stops—pressing the button before reaching the target count $K$. For $K=1$, pressing right after the first round is correct, so performance was spared. But for $K \geq 2$, not a single episode succeeded once pauses or wrist rotations were injected.

The Hidden condition confirms this is not caused by physical disturbance. When the robot paused for 5 seconds or fidgeted its wrist in reality, but those frames were excluded from memory and the clock was held, success rebounded to 45–46 on PickXtimes and 45–47 on SwingXtimes—matching the unperturbed baseline (47 and 44). What disoriented the robot was not physical disruption, but memory recording empty time.

### Spreading Beyond Counting Tasks
This failure is not limited to counting tasks. In demonstration-guided tasks like RouteStick, where a reference video is shown at the beginning, pausing during execution fills the 32 uniform memory slots with useless null frames. This evicts the crucial prompt video frames from memory, causing success to drop sharply from 33 to 7.

captions.F2: Memory breakdown under null events and recovery by hiding them. (a) Illustrations of the three null events, and the difference between Visible (recorded) and Hidden (withheld) memory sampling. (b) Success counts out of 50 episodes. Visible causes catastrophic drops, while Hidden restores performance to the unperturbed baseline (dashed line).

sections.heading: Why it happens: The temporal shortcut born from steady demonstrations
sections.summary: Because demonstration data proceeds at a constant pace, elapsed time alone predicts repetition counts with 80–90% accuracy. Simply rescaling timestamps induces early stopping or over-repetition at will. Furthermore, even models trained without timestamps suffer the same illusion because null event frames occupy memory slots.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Demonstrations Let Time Predict Progress Perfectly
Why does the policy mistake waiting for working? The culprit lies in imitation learning demonstrations, which are collected at a remarkably uniform pace. A simple majority-vote predictor that estimates the completed repetition count purely from elapsed episode steps achieved 89% accuracy on PickXtimes and 80% on SwingXtimes. Real-robot teleoperation data (Open X-Embodiment) shows a similar pattern: regular 3-repetition demonstrations allow progress to be predicted from time with over 92% accuracy. Demonstrations contain no idle waiting, making "reading the clock" the easiest, most powerful shortcut.

### 5.2 Speeding Up the Clock Makes the Robot Stop Early
If the policy truly reads the clock, manipulating timestamps alone should steer its behavior. Without inserting null events or altering image frames, the authors scaled timestamps by $1.5\times$ (running the clock fast). Success plunged from 47 to 18, and all failures were early button presses. Scaling by $0.5\times$ (running the clock slow) caused the robot to repeat extra cycles beyond the target (Figure F4). The policy was undeniably judging task completion by the clock.

### 5.3 Removing Timestamps Does Not Solve It (Slot Occupation)
One might naturally think: why not just remove time embeddings? The authors trained a model from scratch without timestamps, called NoClock. As expected, NoClock became immune to timestamp tampering. Yet when pauses were injected, its success still collapsed to 21 and 14 (Figure F6 a).

The reason is simple: as long as memory uniformly samples 32 frames across the episode, pausing for 5 seconds physically takes up roughly 10 out of the 32 slots with boring, do-nothing frames (Figure F6 b). Controlled experiments showed that the policy infers progress directly from stationary frames occupying memory slots (Figure F6 c). The temporal shortcut lurks not only in timestamps, but in the sequence of time-sampled slots itself.

### 5.4 Comparison Across Memory Designs
Comparing various released RoboMME designs showed that vulnerability directly tracks how memory is indexed. TokenDrop, which keeps tokens with large pixel changes, resists stationary pauses but is fooled by wrist fidgeting where images change violently. In contrast, keyframe memory (such as MemER) and text subgoal memory, which record only when subgoals are completed, successfully shut out null events.

captions.F6: Removing the clock does not prevent failure. (a) NoClock, trained without timestamps, still breaks under two 5-second pauses. (b) Null events enter memory via two paths: explicit timestamp progression and slot occupation across 32 time-sampled slots; NoClock falls for the latter. (c) Injecting empty slots without actual pauses degrades NoClock performance linearly with the number of slots.

sections.heading: Testing the remedies: Data augmentation fails, event-driven indexing works
sections.summary: Data augmentation by adding pauses to training data broke normal counting performance. Conversely, applying an "event-driven index" at inference time—collapsing intervals where the robot and environment return to a prior state into a single frame—recovered more than half the lost success without any retraining.
sections.details:
With the root cause identified, countermeasures boil down to two paths: changing the data (training with pauses) or changing the index (indexing memory by events instead of time).

### Failed Attempt: Pause Augmentation
The authors retrained the policy from scratch with synthetic pauses injected into demonstrations (pause augmentation). However, this backfired. While it seemed to eliminate performance drops under pauses, it did so only because unperturbed baseline performance dropped drastically (PickXtimes dropped to 24 successes). Deprived of time as a reliable crutch, the policy lost the ability to count correctly.

### Highly Effective: Event-Driven Indexing (Event Index)
The alternative approach advances memory based on meaningful events in the world rather than clock ticks. The authors implemented a simple inference-time intervention inspired by loop closure in SLAM:
- **Rule**: If the robot's joint pose matches a previously stored frame, the external scene is unchanged, and no contact or grasp state changed in between, collapse all intervening frames into a single frame (and step) as an empty interval.

Applying this rule at test time using simulator proprioception and contact data more than doubled success rates across pauses, wrist fidgets, and air-grasps **without any additional model training** (SwingXtimes under air-grasp jumped from 13 to 43). Purging meaningless time frames from memory allowed the policy to count events correctly.

However, this approach has a blind spot: legitimate repetitive actions (like releasing a cube and returning to the pick location) also close state loops. This risks mistakenly compressing real progress, highlighting the difficulty of crafting a universal event detector.

sections.heading: Benchmark blind spots and future design guidelines for robot memory
sections.summary: Current memory evaluation benchmarks risk testing mere clock-reading rather than true event recall. Future robot memory should be triggered by state changes in the world (events) rather than clock ticks (time).
sections.details:
### Are Benchmarks Just Testing Clock-Reading Ability?
The revelation that memory benchmarks have degenerated into mere clock-reading tests due to uniform demonstration pacing is a wake-up call for the community. In preliminary experiments on another benchmark, MIKASA-Robo, the authors found that when counting light flashes, policies inferred counts from the total illuminated duration rather than counting discrete flashes. Future memory benchmarks must include standard checks like injecting null events and rescaling clocks.

### What Should Robot Memory Index?
The design principle derived from this study is simple: "Memory should only advance when the world changes." Elapsed time is a convenient proxy, but it runs even when nothing happens. Pixel change handles stationary waiting, but is easily fooled by meaningless wrist shaking. What is truly needed is a mechanism that updates memory triggered by physical events in the world, such as object displacements or contact transitions.

### Limitations of This Study
- Rigorous causal analysis focused primarily on the MME-VLA family; real-robot validation and measuring natural, unscripted null event frequencies remain future work.
- The event index detector relies on ideal simulator contact and segmentation signals; developing equivalent detectors from noisy real-world sensors remains an open challenge.
- The exact visual features (such as similarity or degree of stationarity) that NoClock uses to read progress from slot occupation remain to be fully characterized.

sections.heading: Appendix: Details of wrist fidgets, air-grasps, and extra validation experiments
sections.summary: The appendix provides additional data supporting the paper's claims, including frame visualizations of wrist fidgets and air-grasps, the impact of random micro-stops, and replication on independent architectures (SimpleMemVLA and LTM-pi).
sections.details:
### Frame Visualizations of Wrist Fidgets and Air-Grasps
Figure F9 illustrates frame sequences of wrist fidgets and air-grasps injected during SwingXtimes. From the wrist camera, the wood grain texture rotates dramatically, creating massive pixel-level changes, yet the cube position remains strictly at 0.00 cm. Such noise—moving visually but meaningless for the task—is precisely what misleads time-sampled and pixel-change-based memories most severely.

### Impact of Random Micro-Stops
Beyond long fixed pauses, repeatedly injecting short, random pauses (5 to 40 steps)—mimicking safety layers or network delays—caused similarly severe performance drops. This proves the vulnerability is not an artifact of specific pause timings.

### Validation on Independent Architectures
The authors tested SimpleMemVLA and LTM-$\pi$, which use different backbones. Although these architectures append memory at every step, they exhibited the same tendency to mistake wrist fidgeting for progress and trigger early stops. This confirms that temporal shortcuts are a deep-seated structural issue across memory-augmented policies.

captions.F9: Frame progression during wrist fidgeting and air-grasping. Both front camera (top) and wrist camera (bottom) undergo drastic visual changes, but the cube does not move a single millimeter and the arm eventually returns to its start pose. This is a prime example of visually dynamic motion with zero task progress.

takeaways: Standard VLA memory design (uniform time sampling + timestamps) harbors a fatal shortcut: mistaking idle waiting and wasted motion for task progress via elapsed time.

Because training demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time acts as a powerful progress predictor. Removing timestamps does not solve this, because policies still read time from memory slot occupation.

Data augmentation (injecting pauses) risks destroying baseline counting ability. Instead of palliative training fixes, robot memory requires redesigned indexing triggered by physical events such as contacts and loop closures.
limitations: All causal experiments were conducted in simulation (RoboMME) with scripted null events; quantitative evaluation on spontaneous, real-world null events is not included.
The effective event-driven index relies on ideal simulator contact forces, joint angles, and segmentation; building equivalent event detectors from noisy real-world sensors remains an open challenge.
Repetitive counting tasks face an inherent trade-off: returning to a prior pose after completing a sub-action can be seen as a loop closure, risking accidental erasure of legitimate task history.
